Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference model and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard methods in networks.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a neutron star, interactions between these particles and a pseudoscalar mediator result in the production of standard model particles, namely neutrinos, which could potentially exceed the star's energy output. This process might be visible as a significant emission of neutrinos, detectable with large telescopes like the JWST, and could also influence the star's cooling process. Moreover, the star's crust could be affected by rapid energy releases due to mediating interactions, leading to variations in the star's rotational period over time. This research provides an initial estimate of dark matter particle masses and annotations that would manifest themselves through measurable neutrino signals, as well as changes in the star's rotational period.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in this research, providing a groundwork for extensive cosmological studies when the full 4800 square degree survey is completed. Introducing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge galaxy shape measurement tool, our study leverages the advanced image processing capabilities of the ShapePipe to produce dependable galaxy ellipticity power spectra through the joint analysis of galaxy positions and images. Using multi-band color information to eliminate residual signals, our investigation employs the MultiBand estimator to accurately remove covariant biases in the ellipticity power spectrum, facilitating the cosmological application of second-order anisotropy. Furthermore, we show that combining neighboring bands can minimize bias in the measurement of the ellipticity power spectrum, ultimately enabling the reliable cosmological analysis of the full UNIONS dataset.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from an integer for all integers $n$, the mod $2$ form of $\{q\alpha\}$ will steadily, evenly, and consistently cover the entire interval $(0,1)$ as $q$ progresses through the positive integers. Additionally, we are revisiting and expanding upon some prior results by Lindqvist-Lange and Preiss-Vestrup that address the general application and scope of Veech's discovery, yielding new equity distributions and results based on the tenacity of $\alpha$ to be closely approximated. Furthermore, by leveraging the method used by Preiss-Vestrup to analyze the 1-dimensional Euclidean algorithm, we provide a novel demonstration of its broader applicability to a particular class of general circle rotations, while also revealing connections between its 1-dimensional generalization and results made by Katznelson-Katznelson, Marshall, and Preiss.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2] using different methods.

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin correlations over moderate time scales, which can be observed in NMR measurements. Additionally, a $1/T$ decay of the spin-relaxation time at lower temperatures supports the presence of a BKT phase transition.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model allows for the satisfaction of three key requirements: it matches known neutrino data, solves the strong CP problem, and provides a candidate for dark matter. Within this extended model, we find that, as the axion number changes, a neutrino instability can rapidly transfer normal neutrino fluxes into sterile ones. As a result, an extensive period of neutrino decoupling may have left behind the dark matter we observe today. Using a simplified model involving a narrow resonance, we numerically investigate this process near $Q^* \simeq 2m_N$. Our analysis highlights three compelling cases. First, dark matter composed of right-handed neutrinos could have masses accessible to future direct detection experiments. Second, lighter ($\ll 1$ eV) dark matter might be detectable by means of axion production in upcoming reactor experiments. Third, a small fraction of dark matter consisting of (hidden or open) neutrinos could be within reach of future collider experiments.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from leveraging a recently developed theorem relating the rank of stabilized states to the combinatorial properties of certain binary matrices. Specifically, our analysis confirms that determining the minimum rank of stabilized states involves solving a variant of the minimum weight perfect matching problem, a problem with efficient classical algorithms. This finding allows us to derive upper bounds on the perfect matching problem related to Haar random matrices, which has implications in quantum computing. Moreover, our approach enables the development of a novel classical algorithm for approximating the circuit stabilizer rank, a problem previously explored in quantum computing contexts. The algorithm's performance is supported by theoretical evidence of efficient execution, along with experimental validation in multiple scenarios.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to Quintessence model.
The calculation reveals that the power law exponent and decay rate in the 
non-interacting scenario have a direct relationship, whereas in the interacting scenario,
these parameters demonstrate sensitivity to the interaction term.
Furthermore, in both scenarios, the average value of the effective exponent is 
positive, yet less than zero in the interacting scenario with a negative interaction 
parameter, indicating that these parameters merit further investigation.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra with a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10. This early time-domain research yielded data on numerous moving objects such as 8 RR Lyrae, 57 Cepheid, 0 DL Scu, 9 DO Pho, 3 WW Vir, 9 WW Cet, and 189 other variable stars. It also gathered spectra of about 72 Blazhajskij types and around 58 Delta Scuti stars. Furthermore, it detected or confirmed periodic variations in spectra for about 356 stars and obtained early spectra of around 665 BLANky types. Additionally, it extracted radial velocities for around 28378 stars, which included  processors that had radial velocity variations in around 141 systems.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two commercial FPGA boards. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance with respect to throughput, energy consumption, and latency.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop amplitudes, with a focus on its $d$-dimensional formulation. By examining the properties of causal representation, we identify key constraints that enable the determination of loop structures from the loop-tree duality. Specifically, we investigate the implications of massless internal loops and derive constraints on loop structures in this context. Furthermore, we outline a numerical strategy for evaluating multi-loop amplitudes using causal representation, incorporating numerical integration techniques and recent developments in numerical Gauges. This work builds upon our previous research on the application of loop-tree duality to compute multi-loop amplitudes, a concept first introduced in references [arXiv:1905.07068] and [arXiv:2002.11464].

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Furthermore, for a specified range of $q$, these systems exhibit amplification of the optical signal. By manipulating parameters like tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, one can cause the optical probe to be delayed or advanced by up to milliseconds, with even longer delays achievable through fine-tuning. This work also provides a link between theoretical and physical models, proposing the $q$-deformation as a fundamental anyon model.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate using quantum cluster dynamics to investigate the fluctuations of orbitals and spins at different temperatures. We found that these fluctuations have a significant impact on the thermal diffusivity of the material, with the diffusion constant correlated with the fluctuations of certain orbital patterns. We observed two types of diffusive behaviors, one controlled by spins and a specific orbital pattern, occurring below and above a certain temperature threshold, which was linked to a specific structural change in the material.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers an optimal platform to study such phenomena, primarily due to its distinctive friction force. This interplay between laser cooling and anomalous dynamics is likely to reveal profound and predictive insights into both equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical physics. In experiments involving cold-atom systems, scientists can manipulate and adjust various system parameters to observe changes in the system's behavior, and this has been achieved by analyzing non-normalized states associated with rare events, utilizing tools derived from infinite ergodic theory, resulting in new findings.

Our investigation into cryptocurrency trading links each cryptocurrency pair with
its trading relationships, utilizing a network analysis approach. By applying a
topological framework, we categorize cryptocurrency pairs into distinct groups
based on their network position. In contrast to traditional analyses that focus on
pairwise relationships, our analysis reveals how higher-order interactions influence
price correlations. Furthermore, we revealed a significant connection between
network centrality and price volatility among cryptocurrency pairs.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for certain systems. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water using path integral molecular dynamics at the density functional theory level. Generally, the incorporation of zero-point motion results in the distortion of the mean particle structure, promoting greater proton transfer compared to classical behavior. The incorporation of zero-point motion in the simulation is found to expand the accessible range of proton positions between a sulphuric acid and water molecule at 300K compared to classical predictions, which is further exemplified in other particle configurations.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, which possess totally bounded datasets. Moreover, we present compatibility conditions for these embeddings and demonstrate that they're necessarily satisfied in these specific scenarios.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy potential is also invalid under these circumstances.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, a new class of multivariate probability distribution models, called marginal independence models, is introduced, extending the scope of independence models. It is demonstrated that certain marginal independence models fit within the framework of likelihood models, with a data-driven model known as marginal independence model based on mixed integers (MIMI). The MIMI model serves as a generalization of the independence model based on mixed integers (IMI) and can be identified through a finite number of parameters in various scenarios. Our analysis explores the statistical implications of identifying parameters in MIMI models through both theoretical and practical aspects, with a particular emphasis on covariance matrix estimation in applications. The MIMI model exhibits remarkable success in estimating the covariance matrix of various real-world datasets, often to a precision greater than 90%.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to society. Our model reveals that, under certain conditions, a fair policy may not always prioritize those who would benefit the most. Instead, the model shows a preference towards individuals who have experienced economic difficulties in the past. The model can also represent the likelihood of intergenerational social mobility as a probability distribution. The results suggest that, in the long term, the allocation of opportunities through the system that prioritizes those who have experienced economic difficulties may lead to a more equitable society with greater social mobility opportunities.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the spin-statistics factor through the application of a Pauli transformation. For the non-relativistic context, the relationship between parity and spin-statistics is established through a specific theoretical framework, which does not rely on the properties of angular momentum operators.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using state-of-the-art UD parsing performance on English and Hebrew, and achieves new state-of-the-art results for Hebrew using modern multilingual models. Additionally, the study calls for increased innovation in tasks that were previously done manually, such as named entity recognition and dependency parsing in Hebrew.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $\frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$, and for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, the inequality $ \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} - \varepsilon \leq \|y_i - y_j\|_{\ell_p^d}^p \leq \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} + \varepsilon$ holds. Additionally, an algorithm which computes $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^n$ after taking $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ as input exists and relies on techniques from empirical method and combinatorial theory along with $L_p(\mu)$ factorization theory. It is further

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can enable sequential learning of multiple constitutive laws without memory loss and often with reduced data requirements, matching or exceeding the accuracy achieved through standard training of separate models for each law.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our investigation delves into the effects of altering the size of training corpora on the performance of a large-scale language model (LLaMA) trained on Web texts. We discovered that increasing the training corpus leads to a significant boost in in-context zero-shot task results, but at an expected cost of a substantial rise in required inputs (from 64 to 512 words), accompanied by a notable boost in efficiency (by up to 100 times). Moreover, we found that using a larger training corpus enables the language model to successfully handle more complex tasks, including nuances in semantic text impact assessments and cultural query understanding. One key findings shows that using a larger training corpus results in cleaner data being selected by the language model, resulting in a more accurate task prediction. Interestingly, we noticed that using a larger training corpus results in a shift from using more words from the start of sentences to a greater mixture of sentence position selection, indicating more nuanced data utilization. Furthermore, we found that using a larger training corpus results in higher agreement between replicates, indicating reduced generalization variability.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the role of cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction in the creation and expansion of kiloparsec-scale, filamentary, and sheet-like clouds, we conducted 54 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of galaxy cluster clouds, applying different initial conditions and parameters. Our research indicates that cooling leads to filamentary cloud fragmentation, producing numerous small, gravitationally bound structures. When magnetic fields are strong, they cause clouds to form sheet-like shapes, potentially stabilizing them and hindering the development of small structures. Thermal conduction amplifies the effects of other processes, but can also induce growth in large scales, similar to gas compression. Interestingly, our results show that the typical kiloparsec-scale, filamentary structure observed in galaxy clusters is a transient state, achieved through the balance of opposing forces, but ultimately unstable and short-lived. By analyzing the cloud morphology and growth, we identified four distinct phases, each dominated by different physical processes, and found that the dynamics of these phases are sensitive to parameters like magnetic fields and thermal conduction. Our research demonstrates that galaxy cluster cloud observations are intricate and multifaceted, requiring a deep understanding of the roles of physical processes to accurately interpret their behavior.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and made
the most accurate measurement of this effect within the charm system to date. 
These analyses rely on data gathered from proton-proton collisions in 2011 and
2012, collected by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

With the ascent of the Internet of Things (IoT), cellular networks are expected to experience an exponential expansion in device and energy consumption over the coming years. To prevent over-heating and domain congestion, reliable and efficient energy management in future cellular networks is crucial. To address these issues, we are working on a new series of submissions that present methods for optimizing the operation of next-generation cellular networks from a power perspective. In a recent paper, we have developed an innovative 5G RAN1 power management procedure that enables dynamic adjustment of base station bandwidth and power according to changing user demand. This leads to substantial power savings without affecting user connections or overall system performance. In another paper, we have introduced an IoT-aware tactical power management strategy for next-generation cellular networks, utilizing time-division multiple access (TDMA) scheduling techniques to minimize power consumption while maximizing device throughput. Both these methods accelerate the scaling of future cellular networks and prevent over-heating in mobile equipment. Additionally, we are proposing a set of strategic power management procedures that enable efficient and scalable long-term energy management in next-generation cellular networks, including methods for optimizing power consumption over different service types and scenarios. These procedures are based on a multi-timescale energy management framework that integrates core network management with self-organizing capabilities.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-state regions relate to sonorants. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units using a short-term energy contour as the reference; these units are then grouped based on overlapping sequences in both the spectral and temporal domains, and subsequent representations are generated using a shortened version of the features, and an improved version of the triplet loss. The results show that the proposed system is capable of providing accurate segmentation and underlying graph structure, and delivers a synthesis quality on par with the state-of-the-art in sonorant-focused approaches.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying the "pumped pendulum" model. This analytical model was validated through visual demonstrations and experimental measurements, where the predicted phase differences and amplitude variations matched the observed results. The model also successfully predicted the critical thresholds for tipping over in two and three dimensions, taking into account the initial conditions and time of perturbation.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results are presented to demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD. DR-DSGD exhibits substantial performance improvements over several competing methods in real-world data distribution scenarios.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy nuclear collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma and quark-gluon plasma - black hole duality in the context of high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively low mass each second, whereas those with weaker magnetic fields see high-velocity jets formed regardless of the protostar's mass increase rate. However, in all cases, powerful jets initially drive slower-moving outflows from surrounding material. The efficiency of this're-cycling' process significantly affects how material is redirected from high-velocity jets to outflows, especially when the protostar's mass grows slowly in strongly magnetized clouds. As a result, low-velocity outflows may largely depend on fast-moving jets in these scenarios, implying a crucial relationship where high-velocity jets serve as key drivers for slower-moving outflows.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, certain thresholds can be tolerated for these destabilizing factors, prompting the need for corrective action only when the system's status poses a significant threat. Numerical simulation examples effectively demonstrate the proposed strategy's merits.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and the impact of sunlight pressure. To achieve this, it provides mathematical predictions for the object's equilibrium positions, taking into account its area-to-mass ratio, initial conditions, and the object's variations in eccentricity. Estimates are also developed for the time intervals in which these orbital changes occur, which is crucial in categorizing the object's orbit under different influences. Validation of these estimates was conducted through numerical modeling and the application of specialized tools, such as the Fast Lyapunov Indicator, which helps to identify and visualize patterns related to resonance phenomena. Ultimately, this work aims to lay the groundwork for modeling the impact of sunlight pressure in the framework of established celestial mechanics models, specifically the Extended Fundamental Model, which accounts for key gravitational interactions.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of an object. Our first achievement is developing PACE3D* and PACE2D*, which are novel optimisation algorithms ensuring accurate results for both 3D and 2D keypoint data, through the use of precise mathematical formulations. Additionally, we have developed versions of these algorithms robust to outlier data, labelled PACE3D# and PACE2D#, with a framework called ROBIN for identifying and pruning these errors by utilising a combination of constraints and criteria. Our research also includes thorough testing with various datasets, including the Category-level Object Pose Estimation Challenge benchmark and PASCAL3D+, in order to compare the performance of the novel methods we have created.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach resembles frequentist methods when there's no sharing of data. Notably, by allowing data borrowing, we find smaller trial sizes needed than traditional methods that don't share information. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using two actual trials. Further simulations demonstrate our approach maintains accuracy in detecting positive results without increasing false positives.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulation-based analysis of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, which is prone to variations based on its position.

We introduce a novel deep learning approach, Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration techniques, PRNet leverages deep features to commonize disparate point clouds. Unlike existing methods, PRNet accommodates partial-to-partial registration scenarios by combining two self-supervised learning strategies. Firstly, it employs geometric constraints using overlapping point clouds to derive a global alignment. Secondly, it utilizes a signature-based framework to calculate a similarity score for each pair of points across the registered point clouds. By employing a signature that captures rich geometric content, PRNet's training process is robust against outliers and insensitive to the amount of overlapping data required. Our results show PRNet excels in partial-to-partial registration tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin in overlapping and noisy scenarios. Additionally, PRNet demonstrates superior robustness to parameter variations and a reduced number of required parameters.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal would be to determine the instability scale of the Higgs potential. Achieving this requires reducing uncertainty about two key elements: the Higgs mass and strong coupling constant. Specifically, a 100 TeV collider has the potential to measure the mass of the Higgs with 100 times greater precision and the mass of top quarks with 10 times greater precision. Furthermore, it has the potential to measure the strong coupling constant with 100 times greater precision. In contrast, a 26 TeV LHC has limited potential in these areas, not surpassing the precision found in 2011 predictions. A 33 to 100 TeV FCC hh analysis has the potential to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities, whereas a 26 TeV LHC has very little potential in these areas, not surpassing the precision found in 2011 predictions.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the reliability of experimental data, thus leading to more reliable results. Given its versatility, this technique can easily be applied to a wide range of ultra-fast data from various fields, such as experiment-driven chemistry and physics.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network (CycSGAN) is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. By integrating pre-trained models and eliminating the need for standalone image translation and segmentation steps, CycSGAN significantly reduces the computational cost associated with these operations. Evaluations on the segmentation of neuronal nuclei using EM images and adapting labels between ChestX-ray and MIMIC-Chest X-ray datasets reveal that CycSGAN outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. We present a model that describes the continuum of near-ultraviolet spectral flares in AD Leo, which is supported by data from the Hubble Space Telescope, including observations from the F304, F305, and F309 wavelengths. This model is the first of its kind to utilize spectroscopic data instead of modeling the entire spectrum at once, which is beneficial for identifying features and weaknesses of near-ultraviolet stellar flare models. We also utilized the HST fixed-prism observations of AD Leo to locate a significant change in the line of sight of the target in 1985 and 1989, which facilitated data analysis and comparison of the HST and IUE spectra during a major flare in 1985. Our analysis reveals that a massive solar flare in 1985 had an extreme UV peak and rapid variations, which are comparable to superflares observed in other low-activity stars. Moreover, its profound impact on the optical region of AD Leo, which can serve as a reference point for evaluating similar events in other low-activity stars

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, a significant theorem was put forth previously by Diaconis and Hicks, describing the largest p-core p'-partitions in relation to the smallest walks on the p-ary cube graph. Building upon this work, our research aims to expand the scope of the theorem, making it applicable to a broader set of partitions, which still satisfy the exclusion of elements divisible by p. To achieve this, our work is rooted in the study of the Local Parity Theorem within the context of the p-ary cube graph.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, each radar unit transmits after a randomly generated delay, and we analyze the resulting interference patterns, deriving a metric that quantifies the probability of interference per transmission. This analysis leads to the introduction of a new parameter, illustrating how network throughput varies with this metric. For CSMA, radar units transmit only after detecting that the medium is clear through the detection of a signal with sufficient power, and we find that CSMA generally yields better performance, although there are instances where ALOHA produces superior results. In exploring the effects of parameters, we discover that increasing the number of radar units typically degrades performance, and this is exacerbated in the presence of multiple signal paths. Additionally, we find that CSMA is more susceptible to the effects of multiple signal interference.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model portrays the sample as an energy-preserving spectral filter, aligning with the observed results and providing insight into the entangled two-photon absorption process at zero-phase HOM interferograms.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound is usually not masked in specific situations such as when struck by a heavy object over a hard surface or when struck at a point close to the impact location. An example application is provided that shows how the proposed method can be utilized to synthesize realistic ground sound with parameters adjusted to match those of a virtual reality game.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information technologies.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth lattice in one dimension and the hyper-Pyrochlore lattice across any number of dimensions, extending the principles seen in two-dimensional Kagome and three-dimensional Pyrochlore lattices to higher dimensions.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this compound with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the road to enhancing the critical temperature of hydrogen boride using chemical doping appears to be unfruitful, according to our research.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. Historically, the study of the division of quantities into a few equal parts is associated with the multivariate hypergeometric series, whereas the division of quantities into many equal parts is linked to the Gamma function. In this research, we explore a novel situation that falls outside traditional approaches: distributing a collection of items, characterized by increasing sequential values, into separate, flattened groups according to unique identifiers. We show that such a division results in a distinctive, expressible probability distribution, referred to as the MDMR distribution, by extending the work of Flatto and Shen. We then examine the MDMR distribution's fundamental properties, including moments, asymptotic behavior, and functional relationships. Notably, the MDMR distribution shares a common form of its n-th moment with the K-distribution, as identified by Nadarajah. Our findings are supported by a comprehensive set of numerical examples, which demonstrates the MDMR distribution's applicability in modeling real-world datasets, as well as the convergence of the MDMR distribution to continuous scales, ultimately aligning with renowned probability distributions.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

Highly automated driving systems designed for safe operation include an backup system that steps in when the primary system fails. This backup system, typically based on diverse technology, monitors the primary system to prevent failures and assumes control when necessary. Our study focuses on the safety-critical aspects of this backup system, specifically a fail-safe strategy, and its interaction with the vehicle's dynamics, steering, and braking systems. Using a formal modeling approach, we verify that the backup system can safely switch to the fail-safe position in response to primary system failures, and this approach also considers deviations from the primary system failure mode. Our findings address the uncontrolled failure of the primary system, while evaluations of the vehicle's dynamics and safety are left for future research.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most influential parameters are the matter density, curvature, Hubble constant, and linear HI bias. The accuracy of the parameter estimation is primarily determined by the signal-to-noise ratio that is used to generate the mock data, as well as by the method that is used to remove foregrounds. For a method of foreground removal that reduces the power spectrum by a factor of a few, we find that the estimated parameters show an increase of about 10% to 30% compared to a scenario in which foregrounds are not removed. The scale at which the estimates are most susceptible to changes is roughly between a wavelength of 10 to

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a one-dimensional vector space with an automatically defined linear independence test and an explicitly defined linear independence test.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with deep learning-powered document models by allowing users and items to be influenced by both their interacted neighbors and text-based document models. Additionally, our model offers a unifying structure for existing recommender systems and various data-integrated approaches. We have tested several configurations with popular baseline algorithms on two real-world datasets, which show that our model has superior PPA and MAE performance in both supervised and unsupervised environments.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already present at $O(N^{-3})$. A recently established theory by Pastur and Sinclair extends this to $O(N^{-p})$ for any $p \leq 5$. We now extend this to $O(N^{-p})$ for any $p \leq 7$. Furthermore, we define type $B$ freeness for non-commutative random variables and demonstrate asymptotic type $B$ freeness for unitarily invariant random matrices.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking and that additional isospin breaking arises due to the presence of loops containing kaons, as these do not cancel out when charged and neutral kaon masses differ. A calculated branching ratio for $a_0(980)$ production was found to be on the order of $5 \times 10^{-6}$.
