It is suggested that forthcoming experiments be conducted to investigate this problem, with the ultimate goal of better comprehending scalar resonances through measurements of $\pi^0 \eta$ correlation functions.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, and a $2 \times 2$ camera acquire images of the focused beam; b) a pupil tracker with a lenslet array and a nearby CCD camera capture images of the pupil lens; c) a total of six cameras, each featuring a $3 \times 3$ lenslet array, relay the ordered beams. The camera systems were tested with various measurements including magnification, modulation transfer function, angular resolution, and others, utilizing both artificial and SCALES laboratory experiments with a multi-object shaper. The obtained results demonstrate that the camera provides sufficient resolution to maintain the structural complexity of the VLTI and are in line with the anticipated scientific outcomes of the SCALES project.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] hardness class, in contrast to a proposed efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with doubling dimension values.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways, reducing the required evaluations in two specific scenarios, and introducing a new technique that allows for early termination in the evaluation phase to save computations. This new approach depends on a novel exponential bound for the probability of excessive errors occurring during the process, derived using an entropy-based non-parametric statistical tool.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the ideal gas model's limitations and demonstrating the equation's precision in predicting thermodynamic behaviors. Additionally, a metric has been formulated to determine the critical parameter range in which the ideal gas model and equation of state produce comparable predictions.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and independent of specific network details. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise, detailed information about the PMTs' spectral responses, angular distribution, and other performance features. In the experiment's testing facility, a large number of 20-inch PMTs were tested and analyzed to determine their characteristics. This report presents the findings of those tests, detailing the validated testing methods and documented results.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models, enabling these models to recognize dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration of adaptive graph neural networks significantly boosts model accuracy by an average of 11.6% compared to baseline models.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully applied to industry-level ranking tasks at Baidu.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much larger and unexplored ranges of frequencies. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements, can detect these low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited by bandwidth because low-frequency fluctuations will occur simultaneously at a range of frequencies. In this way, existing sensor networks can be used to experimentally explore the unexplored ranges of the parameter space of this bosonic dark matter.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping techniques and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping to efficiently utilize switch resources. This allows for rapid development and testing of new ideas using public-domain software, with our approach and methodology explained in detail.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that are used to increase the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation, whereas the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach that combines stress tensor and vector-valued displacement to improve spatial accuracy. Both methods were tested and validated using a range of scenarios, including past research data and theoretical outcomes.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model is developed where a scalar field, influenced by third-generation fermions, results in rare transitions between heavy quarks and lighter ones. The nature of its interaction determines the duration of its non-zero state, with a long-lasting phase, unrelated to any particle decay, emerging at lower energy levels. Additionally, a complete analysis of the two-body decay process is performed for all possible diagram combinations, yielding expressions in terms of loop corrections with massless fermions. Applying this model to $b\to s\gamma$ and $b\to d\gamma$ processes yields constraints on the model's parameters by gap values in both cases. Furthermore, exploring the influence of flavor physics effects is also conducted within this model.

Human action understanding in videos has been successfully achieved using Deep Learning models. A new Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) model for video action recognition is proposed, featuring multi-layered attention mechanisms that effectively combine local, contextual, and global features for accurate classification. The HAN model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets, achieving top accuracy with a 59.14% error rate on the former and 26.33% on the latter. Its performance surpasses many recent approaches while requiring significantly fewer parameters, highlighting its efficiency.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analysis, with multiple scenarios showing that the singularity remains confined within the event horizon, thus supporting the cosmic censorship conjecture. In contrast, in a near-extremal black hole, when the scalar field momentum meets a specific condition, the event horizon disappears, and the singularity becomes exposed. Furthermore, this study also shows that a extremal black hole can become non-extremal or extremal again following the interaction with a scalar field.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and helps to explain the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are conducted to evaluate the performance of this method: one with a straightforward harmonic potential, another with a Hardy basis set, and a more complex calculation involving ab initio molecular dynamics simulations. The results show that this method accurately calculates entropy and mutual information with a dependence on the number of samples that follows a theoretical law.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions in this paper involve demonstrating the existence of a particular weak solution with non-negative inventories, classifying all weak solutions as expansion processes, and proving that a weak solution is both unique and optimal when the initial state has a finite number of points. Additionally, we establish the relationship between solutions with non-negative inventories and those with a finite number of points, and provide the explicit expression for the first time a weak solution reaches its maximum inventory level under certain conditions. Furthermore, we expand on a previous result by considering a broader class of solutions with a finite number of points and investigate the behavior of measure-valued solutions with a finite number of points as the time horizon extends indefinitely. Our study also includes a thorough discussion on the relevance of interior points in the support of the initial state.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows exceptional performance in training time and disk usage efficiency while achieving impressive accuracy, outperforming existing light classifiers; for example, it achieved 99\% accuracy in classifying TCP traffic, consuming only 4\% of the memory used by FastNet, a prominent anomaly detection tool.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a new theorem that addresses the existence of a faithful G-action with sub-exponential growth. This is accomplished by demonstrating that any finitely generated solvable group can be represented as a subgroup of a finitely presented one, retaining a sub-exponentially growing action from a related graph.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This research shows that employing ML and AI algorithms alone is not sufficient to fully resolve the problem of simulating complex phenomena such as the falling motions of objects through the use of first-principle models, with the need to advance to a higher level of understanding where secondary physical mechanisms can be accurately represented.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits ranging from 220 to 3600 GeV for certain $R$-hadron masses and 320 to 1970 GeV for long-lived staus or charginos assuming variable lifetimes, representing the most restrictive searches to date for staus and $R$-hadrons in the specified contexts.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by utilizing neat silica substrates for embedding. This design has enabled efficient light collection through the surface and allowed us to achieve high collection efficiency, surpassing 80% in a wide wavelength range. Our research involving quantum dots embedded in silica substrates with different refractive indices has also demonstrated the potential for light propagation in the first mode of the waveguide with very low loss rates. This finding has significant implications for the integration of quantum communication and processing systems.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only enables the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods with a precision of ten times 
less than current methods, suitable for applied physics tasks.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations among eigenvalues derived from integral equations, and in addition, some mode properties are inherently linked with the system's boundary. For specific applications, our results validate the effectiveness of recently proposed methods for enhancing energy within a specified area, and in addition, we predict characteristics of unique mode types such as those focused externally or those that reach deep into a target while scattering may vary widely, their inherent properties remain consistent.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete in solving for individual agent matches. However, finding the best possible stable matches in this more complex format is a complex problem and the capabilities of existing algorithms in achieving such matches are poorly understood.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when the coupling involves position-dependent
velocity of electrons. The presence of a significant valley Hall effect near a
neutral charge condition in the isotropic scenario mirrors that seen with changes
in bond lengths, while in the anisotropic scenario, geometric transport of valleys
is largely mimicked by deformation potentials. The impact of phonon displacement
on valley geometry in the isotropic case resembles that of deformation potential,
although it lacks the contribution of electron velocity. The use of flat bands is
explained as a universal method for understanding how phonon displacement affects
valley geometry. The findings reveal that phonon displacement has a substantial
effect on valley geometry in both situations, yet only produces a minor impact
on valley Hall effect in the anisotropic case.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the directional distances between spaces. This paper demonstrates that any cloud has a central space that represents it, based on certain criteria: the space it resembles must be stable, that is, it remains unchanged under certain distortions; it must also accurately represent the distances of spaces within the cloud. The presence of these central spaces within the cloud also implies the existence of boundaries that separate one cloud from another. The boundaries are formed by spaces that precisely represent the distances of spaces within the cloud, and they also represent the distances of spaces within another cloud, showing that they are, in fact, a transition space.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple single-feed architecture for easy integration with other microstrip circuits. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the desired width, which also ensured stable performance over the specified frequency bandwidth. The input impedance and radiation patterns were closely matched to expectations, with the input impedance stable across the bandwidth at approximately 2.2 ohms. The recorded maximum gain was around 6.5 dB with a consistently wide angle of coverage.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological quantum error correction, which employs a combination of quantum signal processing and logical qubit protection techniques. The current standard quantum error correction approach leverages reinforcement learning, however, recent research has revealed that a different decoder design is necessary to ensure successful fault-tolerant quantum computing. The recent development of the quantum variational cluster operator algorithm has been shown to efficiently achieve a perfect fault-tolerant rate in a small-scale, complex quantum circuit environment. Our research further establishes that the quantum variational cluster operator decoder can be successfully applied at the scale of hundreds of qubits, thereby enabling the construction of a reliable, fault-tolerant quantum computer from quantum-energetic and computational cost perspectives.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These correlations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions show that cold nuclear matter does not significantly influence the phenomena of jet-medium interactions. A comparative analysis with $p$$+$$p$ collisions reveals that cold nuclear matter has no substantial effect on photon-hadron correlations. Furthermore, the suppression of high-energy hadrons linked to the quark-gluon plasma is confirmed, and an estimate of the relative contributions of partonic and statistical nature to this suppression has been made.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and initial state, our results indicate that not using a complete graph to connect qubits can lead to inaccuracies in simulation, although this error can be mitigated by increasing the system size. It's also observed that flaws in initial state preparation don't significantly affect the system's dynamics. Importantly, our simulation demonstrates that the digital-analog method can efficiently simulate fermionic systems, as evidenced by the clear onset of quantum phases in the Fermi-Hubbard model's phase diagram.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they add noise to the gradient signals. We've found that neural networks equipped with additional layers, however, are able to capture more nuanced features related to data variability, including those seen in OoD scenarios. By employing these feature-rich models, the problem of optimizing performance while handling OoD situations can be addressed in a more sustainable manner. Specifically, we've established that rich features enable the development of classifiers that not only excel on the training set, but also consistently score comparably well on the test set, with occasional minor declines. Furthermore, we've found that rich features facilitate the identification of discriminative data characteristics and foster a more adaptable class-conditional distribution. When combined with parameter regularization and a straightforward loss function, rich features also enable the creation of classifiers that are resistant to minor perturbations and domain shifts resulting from in-distribution data. We've supported our claims through an in-depth evaluation of our approach on four domain adaptation and deep learning benchmarks, as well as two external datasets.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissue including fluorescent properties. We've demonstrated the robustness of our proposed integrated system in controlling photon flow into and out of a localized fluorescent dye embedded in tissue. Significant improvements have been achieved over our current best results, yielding an enhanced image clarity, increased conversion efficiency, and reduced convergence time with our WMA-GA and FLC-SLM system. We've obtained an improved image clarity of 57.15, 53.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct methodologies, differences in problem statements, and varying challenge complexities. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the objectivity of our model and explore alternative specifications. In Section 3, we focus on Li (2020) and Liang (2020), examining the pros and cons of our proposed model. In Section 4, we consider Dukes (2020) and Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), evaluating the model through simulated data and thinking through potential limitations in real-world applications.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely slow atmospheric fluctuations. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively utilize the inherent phase information present in the speckle patterns across the image. This innovative system is now ready to be implemented in actual telescopes to enhance their performance and get closer to directly detecting habitable-zone exoplanets.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations are performed, utilizing Monte-Carlo simulations, to showcase the benefits of this model, as evidenced by its similarity to the Hull-White one-factor model's Bermudan swaption prices on Bloomberg, and by its alignment with Bloomberg's constant maturity swap rates.

Research into DUNE's capacity to investigate the connection between eV-fine-tuned sterile and standard neutrinos is underway.
DUNE's potential in this area of study will be discussed in detail, incorporating numerous experimental parameters.
Our investigation demonstrates that, with the aid of a comprehensive LNS-based design, DUNE's sensitivity to neutrino decay and non-standard neutrino interactions is significantly enhanced.
Furthermore, large underground LNS-oriented targets may substantially surpass existing record-low neutrino decay limits established by the MINOS and NUMINOS experiments.
Additionally, our analysis reveals that DUNE's sensitivity to neutrino oscillations related to eV-fine-tuned sterile states is significantly higher than what far-off neutrino experiments can achieve.
In particular, DUNE's first few years of data collection will significantly surpass the current sensitivity thresholds established by the INO and SBNO experiments.

Meta-analyses are often limited by heterogeneity, making it crucial to conduct a pre-defined subgroup analysis to identify potential sources of variation. This analysis presents two new cluster-robust variance estimators designed for mixed-effects meta-regression models that include both continuous and categorical effect variables. Our methodology relies on the assumption that each study's residual variance is normally distributed and independent of its mean. Two variance estimators are proposed, one based on the Hartung-Knapp-Siegel adjustment and the other without adjustment, both of which incorporate effects related to covariates. These estimators are shown to perform well on simulated data and can be used for formal hypothesis testing and confidence interval calculations.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then applied in simulations of individual particles colliding with a wall and as part of a larger simulation involving particle collisions in a channel flow, yielding accurate results that closely aligned with experimental data obtained using traditional models.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to accurately describe measured values, highlighting the success of these models in a new regime corresponding to a high-energy, large-luminosity LHC environment.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This algorithm is specifically designed for use in synchronization primitives, such as locks, and can be integrated into a wide range of other algorithms to enhance robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that the implementation of this algorithm in real systems adds minimal overhead to performance, making it a practical and efficient solution for ensuring the reliability of high-performance computing systems.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we've developed a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, by incorporating symmetry to reduce computation overhead. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of HDTM in navigating vast networks, outperforming alternative models while keeping overhead minimal.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that theoretical models closely matched the measured values for all four measures, demonstrating a great deal of consistency. Furthermore, escape probabilities were found to be influenced by the 0.075 power law, in line with previous findings, while accounting for a long-standing issue regarding the predicted vs. calculated ranges of valid initial conditions. By broadening the range of valid initial conditions, we saw a significant improvement in the match between predicted and calculated escape probabilities.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum in the most central collisions. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the p$_{\rm T}$ range studied.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption of circular symmetry. Analysis of the synchrotron radiation suggests an average polarization level of $\sim 2.5$%, while the forward shock region indicates a nearly 5% polarization. Our model considers both thermal and non-thermal radiation contributions using detailed Chandra data for a spatial-spectral analysis. Our individual pixel search revealed several tentative polarization detections at $\sim 3\sigma$ confidence, indicating considerable turbulence in smaller regions than our current angular resolution allows. Our observations of Cas A indicate that X-ray emission within a radius of $\lesssim 10^{17}$ cm of the forward- and reverse shock regions primarily stems from synchrotron radiation. Our findings i) show IXPE can detect strong polarization signals emanating from regions of high-energy electrons emitting synchrotron radiation, thus validating the capabilities of sensitive X-ray polarization measurements on a small spatial scale, ii) show polarization to be an effective "color" filter to differentiate between synchrotron and other X-ray emission mechanisms in young supernovae, which in turn could use polarization to investigate the "synchrotron catastrophe

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of the Morse-Hamming distance, we divide the interface into multiple components and calculate their reconnection times to establish a universal topological timeline. This allows us to create a general framework for the skeletonization process, making it adaptable to a wide range of interfaces from simple to complex. We represent the dynamics of multi-phase flow interfaces through a topological graph, which provides a clear and interpretable visual representation of their evolution in time. Furthermore, we define a system to describe the topology of these interfaces, which incorporates the linking of interface features across different temporal stages and their correspondence in the spatial domain. This study focuses on the realization that the inherent topology of these interfaces is a robust feature, unaffected by their spatial arrangement or temporal sequence, which allows us to derive a general representation of their dynamics.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies using fluorescence and video analysis. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts and "metabolizes" the carbohydrate surface, generating mechanical movement. In this research, we apply physics-based modeling to explain the underlying physical processes driving this rolling motion, focusing on the conformational changes of hemagglutinin proteins and their interactions with carbohydrates and neighboring virus particles. Our results demonstrate that an essential factor contributing to viral movement is the accumulation of errors in hemagglutinin protein adsorption, leading to increased mechanical stress, as well as the chemical adsorption force acting on the surface. Our study reveals that a critical threshold of adsorption sites must be present on the carbohydrate surface to facilitate viral movement. Additionally, we examine the effect of surface tension and find that viral movement is optimal within a specific range of this tension. Our research explores how factors like virus size, surface coverage, and adsorption force influence viral rolling speed. In contrast to prior models relying on chemical activation, our results show that viral movement can occur through passive mechanisms when the virus undergoes significant conformational changes.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters did not show a correlation with tidal forces or the presence of a companion galaxy. However, they shared similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could cause U-type warping in groups and clusters due to material displaced by RPS forcing galaxies into a U-shape.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, researchers find that this can result in a new crystal structure, F$\bar{4}3$m. Novel materials, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, exhibit no dynamic instability; the inversion symmetry disruption however, leads to phonons with a non-zero total pseudo-angular momentum. Chirally behaving phonons emerge at wave vectors located at the Brillouin zone boundary in both systems under consideration. By exploring this possibility of phonon engineering through doping, researchers open the door for further investigation into the phonon Hall effect and topological heat transport.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our research reveals that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also reveal a connection between the nonadiabatic Born effective charge and the Drude weight in metals, as well as in doped semiconductors, presenting a new perspective on the superconducting mechanism.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, beyond which the fluid's dissipation rate is expected to be significantly affected by random thermal fluctuations. This prediction has far-reaching implications for high-Reynolds number flows, influencing the turbulence's overall structure and properties, including its energy distribution. Moreover, the effect of thermal fluctuations will also impact the large-scale behaviors of fluids, such as the dynamics of geophysical and astrophysical rotations, potentially altering the understanding gained from low-Reynolds number studies. To quantify the dissipation range's transition point, we use numerical simulations of forced turbulence at varying Reynolds numbers, considering scenarios with and without thermal fluctuations. One such simulation reveals that the transition point occurs at a Reynolds number around 40, approximately equivalent to the inverse square root of the Prandtl number. This sheds new light on the, often neglected, influence of thermal fluctuations in high-Reynolds number turbulence and the resulting changes it brings to the turbulence's structure and its energy distribution. Furthermore, these findings also imply significant effects on inertial instability in rotating fluids, potentially transferring power from the mean to fluctuating components, thereby altering previously reported scaling relations.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored in this research. The time-reversal symmetry of this interaction is demonstrated through the creation of a geometric phase equivalent to the Witten effect in a quantum Hall system. Additionally, the concept of a topological magnetoelectric coefficient is applicable to systems without explicit time-reversal symmetry, such as those based on fractional topological insulators, where it takes the form of a half-integer quantum Hall conductance.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, that are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from unstable conclusions on numerous discussion datasets. We then present and compare two methods to enhance design mining accuracy and consistency, with both approaches successfully stabilizing design discussion classifications and producing consistent results in related areas, such as mining discussions to gather information for documentation or design improvement.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Moreover, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber for gravitational waves produced by stars and black holes.
As a result, the absorption of short-scale gravitational waves leads to the emergence of time-reversal symmetry, accounting for the phenomenon of gravity as experienced on Earth.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in a significantly improved convergence rate for specific nondegenerated nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems. Moreover, our algorithm is accompanied by a numerical study that includes optimizations regulated by $\ell_1$-norm and trace-norm.

This research aims to examine weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within the context of commutative rings and extend the Prim-Charternbonn's theorem. We contend that an ideal $I$ off a commutative ring $R$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal if and only if for any three-ring elements $a,b,$ and $c$, where $aRb \subseteq I$, then $acr$ or $br \in I$ for all $r \in R$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an ideal $I$ off a commutative ring $R$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal if and only if for any three-ring elements $a,b,$ and $c$, where $aRb \subseteq I$, then $ac \in I$ or $br \in I$ for all $r \in R$. We also establish that an ideal $I$ off a commutative ring $R$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal if and only if for any two-ring elements $a$ and $b$, where $ab \in I$, then $a \in I$ or $b \in I$. Moreover, we find some examples and corollaries to support our research findings.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider at $\sqrt{s}=7$ GeV, where the recoil $B$ meson is fully reconstructed through hadronic decays. Our analysis includes partial reconstruction of $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a muon-neutrino pair, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and an electron-antineutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ and a muon-neutrino pair, and these processes result in observed yields, 53 counts with a statistical significance of 5.3 sigma, 25 counts with a statistical significance of 4.8 sigma, and 28 counts with a statistical significance of 4.8 sigma, respectively. Our analysis also includes signal yield upper limits for three additional decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a muon-neutrino pair, $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ and an electron-antineutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects. We outline a method to create such photonic devices, illustrate our findings with photonic research examples, and discuss their potential applications in astronomical research and their current state along with future prospects.

In the last few years, various machine learning approaches have emerged with the aim of pharmaceutical partnerships prediction. This task is crucial not only to understand disease causation but also to control side effects by monitoring drug interactions. Although significant progress has been achieved so far, no comprehensive overview of this field has been implemented which would be crucial to further advancement in this domain. In order to fill in this knowledge gap, this paper aims to provide an all-encompassing survey of recent developments in this domain by highlighting the strengths and weaknesses, as well as examining the previously unexplored areas for future studies.

Several local governments have shown interest in using Deep Learning (DL) for
automating the process of detecting road damage but face obstacles in securing
sufficient data for training. To overcome this challenge, this study leverages
transfer learning, applying a pre-trained and widely-used Deep Neural Network to
road scene images from the Netherlands, Japan, Germany, Indonesia, and Mexico.
Our team has developed an innovative solution to address two key problems: the
limited availability of labeled data and the need to adapt a model to multiple
different countries. To resolve these issues, we have created a dataset of 4000
labeled images from various countries and developed a new technique for
fine-tuning a pre-trained model using a reduced number of labeled samples. The
study evaluates several state-of-the-art Deep Neural Networks and compares their
performance using different dataset combinations from the respective countries.
The results show that a pre-trained ResNet-18 model can effectively detect road
damage with an accuracy of 94% using data from three distinct countries. This
